'''Reiner Kümmel''' (born 9 July 1939)<ref name="dissertation"/> is a German physicist specialised in [[solid-state physics]], [[thermodynamics]] and [[econophysics]].<ref name="CV">{{cite web
|date        = 2013-10-09
|title       = Prof. Dr. Reiner Kümmel
|url         = http://www.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/institute_einrichtungen/institut_fuer_theoretische_physik_und_astrophysik/theoretische_physik_i/tp_i/mitarbeiter/prof_dr_em_reiner_kuemmel/
|publisher   = Universität Würzburg
|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140109105130/http://www.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/institute_einrichtungen/institut_fuer_theoretische_physik_und_astrophysik/theoretische_physik_i/tp_i/mitarbeiter/prof_dr_em_reiner_kuemmel/
|access-date = 2025-01-10
|archive-date = 9 January 2014
}}</ref><ref>
{{cite book
|first=Kishore C. |last=Dash
|chapter=14 Evolution of Econophysics
|quote=Reiner Kümmel [Short CV] |page=261
|editor-first1=Frédéric	|editor-last1=Abergel
|editor-first2=Hideaki	|editor-last2=Aoyama
|editor-first3=Bikas K.	|editor-last3=Chakrabarti
|editor-first4=Anirban	|editor-last4=Chakraborti

== Scientific career ==
Reiner Kümmel studied physics and mathematics at [[Technische Universität Darmstadt|TH Darmstadt]] from 1959 to 1964. He received a scholarship from the [[Cusanuswerk]] and completed his doctorate on [[superconductivity]] at [[Frankfurt University]] in 1968,<ref name="dissertation">{{cite thesis |first=Reiner |last=Kümmel |title=A: Schichtdicken-abhängiger Quantisierungseffekt in Tunnelkontakten – B: Untersuchungen zum Zwischenzustand und gemischten Zustand von Supraleitern 1. und 2. Art |url=https://d-nb.info/481533435 |trans-title=A: Layer thickness dependent quantisation effect in tunnel contacts – B: Investigations on the intermediate state and mixed state of superconductors of the 1st and 2nd kind |language=de |location=Frankfurt am Main |publisher=Goethe-Universität Frankfurt |date=1968 |access-date=2025-01-10}}</ref> where he also habilitated in theoretical physics in 1973. During his doctorate and [[habilitation]], he also conducted research abroad, such as from 1965 to 1967 as a research assistant under the two-time Nobel Prize winner in physics [[John Bardeen]] at the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign|University of Illinois]] at [[Champaign–Urbana metropolitan area|Urbana-Champaign]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kümmel |first1=Reiner |last2=Landwehr |first2=Gottfried |date=1991 |title=In memoriam John Bardeen |journal=Physikalische Blätter |volume=47 |issue=5 |publisher=Wiley-VCH |pages=399–400 |doi=10.1002/phbl.19910470512 |doi-access=free }}</ref> From 1970 to 1972, he worked in Colombia at the [[University of Valle|Universidad del Valle]] in [[Cali]],<ref name="CV" /> where he helped to set up a master's programme in physics on a [[German Academic Exchange Service|DAAD]] scholarship, which served to develop the next generation of academics. During this time, he focussed on [[thermodynamics]].<ref>{{cite journal  |first1=Marcos G. E. |last1=da Luz |date=2011-12-01 |title=The Second Law of Economics: Energy, Entropy, and the Origins of Wealth |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article/64/12/57/413528/The-Second-Law-of-Economics-Energy-Entropy-and-the |journal=Physics Today |ISSN=1945-0699 |volume=64 |issue=12 |publisher=American Institute of Physics |pages=57 |quote=For more than 30 years, Kümmel has been at the forefront of the study of economic thermodynamics, which considers the relationship of the natural sciences to economics—thermodynamics and economics are bridged by the constraints that thermodynamic laws place on natural-resources availability and economics-based environmental preservation. |doi=10.1063/PT.3.1366 |access-date=2025-02-21|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 1974, he took up a professorship for [[theoretical physics]] in [[University of Würzburg|Würzburg]], which was also characterised by numerous research visits abroad. In the 1970s, the time of the first and second [[1970s energy crisis|oil price shocks]], his interest in economics as a second mainstay began to grow. A lively exchange developed with Wolfgang Eichhorn, who worked as an economist (and mathematician) at the Faculty of Economics at the [[University of Karlsruhe]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kümmel |first1=Reiner |last2=Strassl |first2=Wolfgang |last3=Gossner |first3=Alfred |last4=Eichhorn |first4=Wolfgang |title=Technical progress and energy dependent production functions Articles |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01282565 |journal= Journal of Economics |volume=45 |publisher=Springer |date=1985 |pages=285–311 |doi=10.1007/BF01282565 |access-date=2025-01-11|url-access=subscription }}</ref> His research in physics focussed on the theory of inhomogeneous [[superconductors]] and [[Mesoscopic physics|mesoscopic heterocontacts]].<ref>{{cite web |first = Reiner |last = Kümmel |title = Welcome to the pages of Prof. Dr. Reiner Kümmel |url = https://pawn.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/~kuemmel/English/indexE.html |publisher = Fakultät für Physik und Astronomie, Universität Würzburg |access-date = 2025-01-10}}</ref> His economic interests focussed on energy use and emission reduction. From 1996 to 1998, Reiner Kümmel chaired the Energy Working Group of the [[German Physical Society]].<ref>{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |date=2024-05-15 |title=Arbeitskreis Energie (AKE) |url=https://www.dpg-physik.de/vereinigungen/fachuebergreifend/ak/ake/kontakt |website=www.dpg-physik.de |location=Bad Honnef |publisher=[[Deutsche Physikalische Gesellschaft]] |access-date=2025-01-10 |quote=Vorsitzende seit Gründung des Arbeitskreises}}</ref> He retired in October 2004 from University of Würzburg. Nevertheless, he remained associated with the university with a teaching assignment for the lecture ''Thermodynamics and Economics''<ref>{{cite book |first=Reiner |last=Kümmel |title=Energie und Wirtschaftswachstum oder: Wie Arbeitslosigkeit und Umweltbelastungen vermindert werden können |url=https://pawn.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/~kuemmel/wachstum.pdf |trans-title=Energy and economic growth or: How unemployment and environmental harm can be reduced |language=de |location=Würzburg |publisher=Würzburg University |date=2007-03-24 |access-date=}}</ref> until the summer semester 2015.<ref>{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |date=2015-04-14 |title=Sommersemester 2015 – Thermodynamik und Ökonomie: Energie und Wirtschaftswachstum, Entropieproduktion und Emissionsminderung |url=https://pawn.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/~kuemmel/lehre.html |location=Würzburg |publisher=Würzburg University, Department of Physics |access-date=2025-01-10}}</ref> He is a member of the editorial board of ''Biophysical Economics and Sustainability''.<ref>{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |title=Editorial board |url=https://link.springer.com/journal/41247/editorial-board |work=Biophysical Economics and Sustainability |location=Heidelberg |date=2025 |publisher=Springer Nature |access-date=2025-01-19}}
</ref>

== Work ==
Kümmel's work on economics intends to improve the mathematical structure of [[exogenous growth model|macroeconomic growth models]] for industrial countries, so that they do not contradict the fundamental laws of physics, in particular the first and second law of thermodynamics. He identified energy as a powerful factor of production and the dominant component of technological progress.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hall |first1=Charles |last2=Lindenberger |first2=Dietmar |last3=Kümmel |first3=Reiner |last4=Kroeger |first4=Timm |last5=Eichhorn |first5=Wolfgang |date=2001-08-01 |title=The Need to Reintegrate the Natural Sciences with Economics |url=https://bpeinstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Hall_2001_etal_Reintegrate-2019_06_27-16_10_21-UTC.pdf |journal=BioScience |volume=51 |issue=8 |publisher= Oxford University Press |pages=663–673 |doi=10.1641/0006-3568(2001)051[0663:TNTRTN]2.0.CO;2 |access-date=2025-01-13 |quote= Past criticisms of neoclassical economics from the perspective of natural scientists can be summarized as three fundamental arguments: (1) The structure of the basic conceptual neoclassical model is unrealistic because it is not based on the biophysical world and the laws governing it, especially thermodynamics (Figure la); (2) the boundaries of analysis are inappropriate because they do not include the real processes of the biosphere that provide the material and energy inputs, the waste sinks, and the necessary milieu for the economic process (Figure 2); and (3) the basic assumptions underlying the models used have not been put forth as testable hypotheses but rather as givens. |quote-page=664}}</ref> To address these issues amongst others, he developed the so-called LINEX function, which depends linearly on energy and exponentially on quotients of the production factors capital, labor, and energy.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Lindenberger |first1=Dietmar |last2=Kümmel |first2=Reiner |date=2002 |title=Energy-Dependent Production Functions and the Optimization Model "PRISE" of Price-Induced Sectoral Evolution |journal=International Journal of Thermodynamics |s2cid=67765773 |language=en}}</ref>

The LINEX production function is calculated by integrating the growth equation for economic output and three coupled differential equations for the economic weights of capital, labor, and energy, i.e. the output elasticities. These are subject to constant returns to scale (Euler condition) and appropriate asymptotic boundary conditions. The LINEX function forgoes the cost-share theorem applied in standard economic theory. This theorem assumes that the economic weights ([[Elasticity (economics)|elasticities]]) of capital, labor and energy are equal to their cost-shares in the [[national accounts]] and [[national statistics]], respectively.<ref>{{cite book |first1=Michael |last1=Kumhof |first2=Dirk V |last2=Muir |date=2012-10-25 |title=Oil and the World Economy: Some Possible Futures |series=IMF Working Papers |url=https://www.elibrary.imf.org/downloadpdf/view/journals/001/2012/256/001.2012.issue-256-en.pdf |location=Washington D.C. |publisher=International Monetary Fund |page=14 |isbn=9781475586640 |access-date=2025-01-24 |quote=For the contribution of oil to GDP, the main problem is that conventional production functions imply an equality of cost shares and output contributions of oil. This has led economists to conclude that, given its historically low cost share of around 3.5% for the U.S. economy, oil can never account for a massive output contraction [..] several recent articles and books by natural scientists have argued that output contributions of energy/oil need not equal cost shares with a more appropriate modeling of the aggregate technology.}}</ref> Thus capital and labor would be the main [[factors of production]]; as such they appear in the constant output elasticities of the often-used [[Cobb–Douglas production function]], which is the simplest solution of the differential equations. The time-dependent parameters in the output elasticities of the LINEX function are determined econometrically using statistical methods.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ayres |first1=Robert U. |last2=Warr |first2=Benjamin |date=2005-06-01 |title=Accounting for growth: the role of physical work |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0954349X03000778 |journal=Structural Change and Economic Dynamics |series=Contains the special issue Approaches to Production Theory |volume=16 |issue=2 |pages=181–209 |doi=10.1016/j.strueco.2003.10.003 |issn=0954-349X|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ayres |first1=Robert U. |last2=van den Bergh |first2=Jeroen C. J. M. |last3=Lindenberger |first3=Dietmar |last4=Warr |first4=Benjamin |date=2013-12-01 |title=The underestimated contribution of energy to economic growth |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0954349X13000593 |journal=Structural Change and Economic Dynamics |volume=27 |pages=79–88 |doi=10.1016/j.strueco.2013.07.004 |issn=0954-349X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Kümmel, and colleague Dietmar Lindenberger first fit the LINEX function using electricity as a proxy for the [[useful work]] from energy inputs.<ref name=":0" /> The resulting fits were able reproduce observed historical economic growth without assumptions of exogenous and unexplained technological progress. In subsequent work, inspired and informed by Kümmel's findings, [[Robert Ayres (scientist)|Robert Ayres]] and Benjamin Warr replaced electricity in the function with the [[useful work]] from [[exergy]] inputs to the US economy (for the period 1900 to 2000) to the LINEX production function to similar effect.

With the use of [[useful work]] as input factor, the unexplained growth the "[[Solow residual|Solow Residual]]" from [[Solow Growth Model|Solow's growth model]], which is often attributed to exogenous technological progress or [[total factor productivity]], is minimised.<ref>{{cite book |last=Rifkin |first=Jeremy |author-link=Jeremy Rifkin |date=2014 |title=The Zero Marginal Cost Society – The Internet of Things, the Collaborative Commons, and the Eclipse of Capitalism |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=L6afAgAAQBAJ&pg=PT72 |location=New York, NY |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan |page=72 |isbn=978-1137278463 |access-date=2025-01-14 |quote= Over the past 25 years, a number of analysts, including physicist Reiner Kümmel of the University of Würzburg, Germany, and economist Robert Ayres at INSEAD business school in Fontainebleau, France, have gone back and retraced the economic growth of the industrial period using a three-factor analysis of machine capital, labor performance, and thermodynamic efficiency of energy use. [..] In other words, 'energy' is the missing factor.}}</ref> Consequently, so called ''technological progress'' in neoclassical models can be explained, in large part, as the ability of mankind to integrate increasing energy flows into the economic process and to transform it with high efficiency into [[useful work]].<ref>{{cite book
|author-first1=Thomas |author-last1=Homer-Dixon |author-first2=Nick |author-last2=Garrison |chapter=Introduction |editor-last=Homer-Dixon |editor-first=Thomas |editor-link=Thomas Homer-Dixon |title= Carbon shift - How the twin crises of oil depletion and climate change will define the future |others=foreword by Ronald Wright
|isbn= 978-0-307-35718-2 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k8dNQUm7hlIC
|publisher=Random House |location=Canada |date=2009 |pages=6–7 |access-date=2025-01-15
|quote=Often overlooked was the role of energy in economic growth. [..] Growth was invariably much higher than he [Solow] predicted, and the difference – that proportion of output growth that could not be explained by the measured inputs – came to be called the 'Solow residual.' But as economist Reiner Kümmel later pointed out, this residual often explains more than Solow's thery itself. After Solow's work, it had been widely assumed that the 'something else' that combines with labour and capital to produce economic growth must be technology. [..] But by counting energy inputs in terms of joules rather than dollars, Kümmel not only produced results matching real-world growth rates and nearly eliminated the Solow residual, he also clarified the importance of energy to the economy.}}</ref> It then follows that energy's economic weight is much larger than its cost share, and that energy is a powerful factor of production and a dominant component of "technological progress". As Kümmel states "''we owe a substantial part of our material wealth to energy conversion in the machines of the capital stock''".<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kümmel |first=Reiner |date=2013-12-01 |title=Why energy's economic weight is much larger than its cost share |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S2210422413000634 |journal=Environmental Innovation and Societal Transitions |series=Energy, materials and growth: A homage to Robert Ayres |volume=9 |pages=33–37 |doi=10.1016/j.eist.2013.09.003 |issn=2210-4224|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In his book ''The Second Law of Economics'', he discusses the influence of energy conservation and entropy on prosperity and adds to the production theory of economics the important scientific component of energy, without which a modern economy cannot be understood.<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Mimkes |first1= Jürgen |date=2012 |title= The Second Law of Economics |language=de |url=https://pro-physik.de/zeitschriften/download/13596 |department=Book Review |journal= Physik Journal |issn=1617-9439 |volume=11 |issue=6 |publisher= Wiley-VCH|pages=67 |access-date=2025-01-13}}</ref> He calls for [[energy tax]]es to [[The Limits to Growth|alleviate the pressure to grow]], based on the much higher production elasticity of energy than labour. The current trend is the replacement of labor-capital combinations by energy-capital tuples.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zyga |first1=Lisa |date=2014-12-31 |title=Thermodynamic analysis reveals large overlooked role of oil and other energy sources in the economy |url=https://phys.org/news/2014-12-thermodynamic-analysis-reveals-large-overlooked.html |work=Phys.org |publisher=Omicron Ltd. |access-date=2024-01-24 |quote=On the other hand, cheap, powerful energy-capital combinations are increasingly replacing expensive, weak labor in the course of increasing automation. This combination kills jobs for the less skilled part of the labor force. [..] This well-known trend can be understood by the new model's message that energy is cheaper and more powerful than labor.}}</ref>

== Impact beyond academia ==
Kümmel's economic work has been featured and cited by a variety of organizations, particularly as it relates to [[energy policy]]. In 1990, the [[World Bank]] featured Kümmel's work on the economics of pollution control in its Environment Working Paper series.<ref name="WorldBank_1990">{{Cite report |url=https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/861571538250112806/pdf/The-ecological-economics-of-sustainability-making-local-and-short-term-goals-consistent-with-global-and-long-term-goals.pdf |title=The Ecological Economics of Sustainability: Making Local and Short-Term Goals Consistent with Global and Long-Term Goals |last1=Costanza |first1=Robert |last2=Haskell |first2=Ben |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240918131230/https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/861571538250112806/pdf/The-ecological-economics-of-sustainability-making-local-and-short-term-goals-consistent-with-global-and-long-term-goals.pdf |archive-date=2024-09-18 |website=documents1.worldbank.org |series=Environment Working Papers |department=Environment Department}}</ref> The [[International Monetary Fund]] of the [[United Nations]]
